entry.def: The speed of the beat. It is shown by an Italian word such as allegro, by a metronome mark, or by both.

entry.gloss: the tempo in beats per minute
entry.def: A tempo given exactly as a note value and a number of beats per minute: a quarter note = 60 means sixty quarter-note beats in a minute, one each second. M.M. stands for Maelzel's metronome.
Very slow and broad; the word means broad. Larghetto, a little broad, is somewhat less slow.
Slow. Composers have not agreed on the order of the slow terms largo, lento and adagio, so treat them as roughly equally slow.
Slow; the word means at ease. It is slower than andante.

At a walking pace, from the Italian andare, to walk: a moderate, flowing tempo, slower than moderato. Andantino, a little andante, is today usually taken as a little faster than andante, but in the 18th century it could also mean a little slower.
At a moderate speed, between andante and allegro. It also tempers another term: allegro moderato is moderately fast.
Fairly fast: a little slower and usually lighter than allegro.
Fast and lively; the word means cheerful. It is the most common fast tempo.
Lively and quick. Today it usually means faster than allegro, but in Baroque music it often describes a lively character at a more moderate speed.
Very fast, faster than allegro. Prestissimo means as fast as possible.
With movement: flowing, a little faster than the tempo word alone would suggest, as in andante con moto.
Getting gradually faster.
Getting gradually slower; the word means delaying. Also abbreviated ritard.

entry.gloss: slowing down little by little, like ritardando
entry.def: Getting gradually slower; the word means slowing down. In practice it means the same as ritardando.
Held back: slower straight away rather than gradually, unlike ritardando. Because rit. normally stands for ritardando, ritenuto is abbreviated riten.
In time: return to the tempo that was in use before a change such as a ritardando or an accelerando.
Freely stretching and pressing the tempo for expression, lengthening some notes and shortening others while the music keeps its sense of pulse. From tempo rubato, robbed time.

entry.gloss: hold longer than the written value
entry.def: A curve with a dot under it, written over a note or rest: hold it longer than its written value, for as long as the performer or conductor chooses. Called a pause in British English.

entry.gloss: loudness and the signs that show it
entry.def: How loud or soft music is, and the signs that show it: letters such as p and f, words such as crescendo, and hairpins.
Very soft, softer than piano. Even softer levels are written ppp.
Soft. The instrument's name is short for pianoforte, soft–loud, because it could play both.
Moderately soft, between piano and mezzo-forte; mezzo means half.
Moderately loud, between mezzo-piano and forte.
Loud; the word means strong.
Very loud, louder than forte. Even louder levels are written fff.

entry.gloss: a sudden strong accent on one note
entry.def: Forcing: a sudden, strong accent on a single note or chord, written sfz or sf. How strong it is depends on the dynamic around it.
Loud and then at once soft: the note begins forte and drops straight to piano. The same word is also a name for the early piano.
Getting gradually louder. Written as the word, the abbreviation, or a hairpin opening to the right.
Getting gradually softer; decrescendo means the same. Written as the word, the abbreviation, or a hairpin closing to the right.

entry.gloss: how notes are begun, joined or separated
entry.def: How notes are started, connected and separated, and the signs that show it, such as staccato dots, accents and slurs.
Detached: the note is shortened, leaving a gap before the next one, without changing the rhythm. Shown by a dot above or below the notehead, on the side away from the stem.
Smoothly connected, with no gap between the notes; the word means bound. Shown by a slur or by the word.

entry.gloss: stressed more than the notes around it
entry.def: A sign shaped like > above or below a note: play it with more emphasis than the notes around it.
Held: a short horizontal line above or below a note asks for its full value, often with a slight stress.
Marked: played with a strong accent. Shown by the word or by a sign shaped like ^ above the note, a stronger accent than >.

entry.gloss: curved line over notes to be played legato
entry.def: A curved line over or under two or more notes of different pitches, which are played legato: string players take them in one bow, and wind players tongue only the first note. A curve joining two notes of the same pitch is a tie.
Sweetly: soft and gentle in tone.
In a singing style: with a smooth, flowing line that brings out the melody.
Expressively, with feeling.
Gracefully, with elegance.
Majestically: stately and dignified, usually at a broad tempo.
Very, much: molto allegro is very fast and molto rit. slows down a lot.
A little: poco rit. means slowing down slightly.
Little by little, gradually: cresc. poco a poco asks for a slow, steady build in loudness.
More: più forte is louder and più mosso, with more motion, is faster.
Less: meno mosso, with less motion, is slower and meno forte is less loud.
Always, throughout: sempre staccato means keep playing staccato.
Suddenly, immediately: subito piano means become soft at once.
Not too much: allegro ma non troppo means fast, but not too fast.

From the beginning: go back to the start of the piece. D.C. al fine means repeat from the beginning and stop at fine; D.C. al coda means repeat from the beginning to the coda mark, then jump to the coda.
From the sign: go back to the segno, a slanted S with a line and two dots, and play on from there, to fine (D.S. al fine) or to the coda mark (D.S. al coda).

entry.gloss: the end, after a da capo or dal segno
entry.def: The end: marks where the piece finishes after a da capo or dal segno, which may be before the last bar on the page. An Italian word, pronounced in two syllables.
A closing section added at the end of a piece or movement; the word means tail. In a da capo or dal segno repeat, the coda mark, a circle crossed by two lines, shows where to jump to the coda.
